html:
The move of two master painters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, from the court of Safavid Iran to the Mughal emperor Humayun, who brought them to India in 1555. Their workshop gave birth to Mughal painting.

Humayun, son of Babur, had lost his throne to Sher Shah Suri and fled to Iran in 1544, where Shah Tahmasp gave him refuge. There he saw the finest book painting of the age, the Persian miniature. The shah was losing interest in painting, and Humayun invited the two artists. They joined him in Kabul and came with him when he won back Delhi in 1555.

Humayun died the next year, but his son Akbar gave them charge of a large royal workshop of Indian artists, Hindu and Muslim. Their first great task was the Hamzanama, a giant illustrated book of the adventures of Amir Hamza. Out of this mix grew a new style: Persian line and colour joined Indian liveliness and later European ideas of depth, and painters began to paint real people, animals and court life.
sum: The move of two master painters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, from the court of Safavid Iran to the Mughal emperor Humayun, who brought them to India in 1555. Their workshop gave birth to Mughal painting.
